steps.title: One term
steps.idea: Start with one random variable $X$, here an exponential waiting time. Its law is lopsided: most values are small, a few are large.

layers.intuition: Each dot that falls is one value of $X$. They pile up near zero, exactly where the density is high.
layers.definition: All the theorem asks of one term: an expectation $a = MX$ and a finite variance $\sigma^2 = DX > 0$.

steps.title: Many independent terms
steps.idea: Take $n$ independent copies $X_1, \dots, X_n$ of the same law. Each one falls into its own slot of the machine.

steps.title: The sum
steps.idea: The machine adds the terms up. The sum $S_n$ drifts away and spreads out as $n$ grows: its mean is $na$ and its variance $n\sigma^2$.

layers.details: Expectation is always additive. Variance is additive for independent terms: $D(X_1 + \dots + X_n) = DX_1 + \dots + DX_n = n\sigma^2$, so the spread of $S_n$ grows like $\sigma\sqrt{n}$.

steps.title: Centre and scale
steps.idea: To compare sums of different length, subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. The result $z$ always has mean $0$ and variance $1$; only its shape can change.

layers.intuition: The gate in the middle of the machine does exactly this: it shifts every bead by $na$ and shrinks it by $\sigma\sqrt{n}$.

steps.title: Thousands of sums
steps.idea: Repeat the whole experiment thousands of times. Every standardized sum drops into the histogram. Its shape no longer looks like the exponential law.

layers.intuition: With $n = 1$ the histogram is the exponential law itself, only shifted and scaled. Add terms and the long right tail melts away.

steps.title: The central limit theorem
steps.idea: As $n$ grows, the law of $z$ approaches the standard normal law, whatever the law of one term, as long as its variance is finite. This is the Lindeberg–Lévy theorem.

layers.intuition: Every term pushes the sum a little left or right. With many small independent pushes the details of one push wash out; only its mean and variance survive. That is why the bell is universal.
layers.definition: Lindeberg–Lévy: if $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are independent, identically distributed, $MX_k = a$ and $0 < DX_k = \sigma^2 < \infty$, then $P\left(\frac{S_n - na}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} < x\right) \to \Phi(x)$ for every $x$.
layers.details: Through characteristic functions (lecture 9): $\varphi_z(t) = \left(\varphi_{X - a}\!\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right)\right)^{n} = \left(1 - \frac{t^2}{2n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right)^{n} \to e^{-t^2/2}$, the characteristic function of $N(0, 1)$. The yellow number is the Kolmogorov distance; it falls toward the Monte Carlo noise of 4000 sums, about $0.03$.

steps.notes: Ask the room to predict the histogram for $n = 1$ before clicking the chip.

steps.title: Three sources, one limit
steps.idea: Run three factories side by side: a uniform term, an exponential term and a coin. Single terms look nothing alike, yet the standardized sums meet at the same bell. The skewed ones arrive later.

layers.details: Berry–Esseen: the distance to $\Phi$ is at most $C\,\dfrac{M|X - a|^3}{\sigma^3\sqrt{n}}$. A skewed or rare-event term has a large third moment, so it needs a larger $n$.

steps.title: Lyapunov condition
steps.idea: The terms need not share one law, as long as no single term dominates the sum.

experiment.label: Distance to the normal law against $n$
